questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The order of the eradication work
questions.learningObjective: State the correct order for removing a confirmed compromised process.
questions.stem: In tonight's observatory log the north dome laptop ran a script that is not on the approved list. Which sequence eradicates it correctly?

options.text: Remove the unauthorised script, then hunt for persistence, then rebuild from a known-good image.
Reimage the laptop first, then reconnect to the dome network and see whether the script returns.
options.misconception: believes rebuilding the laptop removes the persistence

options.text: Run a full scan, let it quarantine what it finds, then resume the night's observing run.
options.misconception: assumes a quarantine action proves nothing is left

options.text: Disconnect the laptop from the dome network and deal with it properly at the next session.
options.misconception: treats isolation as if it were a complete removal

questions.explanation: Removal comes first, then persistence checks, then rebuild. Quarantine alone leaves the foothold on disk and isolation alone leaves the script waiting to run again.
questions.hint: Ask what must still be hunted for after the process is gone.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why removing one process is not the end of it
questions.learningObjective: Interpret evidence that removing one process did not end the intrusion.
questions.stem: The entry for 3 September records one malicious script removed at 22:14, yet outbound connections continued until 04:40 the next morning. What does that show?

options.text: The removal worked, since the script itself no longer runs on the machine any more.
options.misconception: equates a stopped script with a cleared system

options.text: The dome network was down, which explains the delay before the connections stopped.
options.misconception: blames network downtime for the surviving activity

options.text: Other surviving parts of the intrusion were still active, so the removal did not finish the job.
Those connections belong to the mount control software and are a normal nightly pattern.
options.misconception: assumes recurring traffic is always benign

questions.explanation: Removing one process leaves the access that started it in place. Traffic that continues after the removal shows the intruder was wider than the one script in the log.
questions.hint: Look at what was still happening after the removal.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why bringing the service back is not the end
questions.learningObjective: Explain why restoring a service does not by itself close an incident.
questions.stem: The observatory booking system was back online on 14 May after a week of cleaning. Explain why restoring it did not by itself close the incident.

answer.exemplar: Restoration only shows that the service can run again. It does not show that every foothold was removed, that the route used to gain access has been closed, or that the same entry cannot be used again tomorrow. Closing an incident also needs the eradication steps verified and the timeline written down for later review.

questions.explanation: A service can work while the access that broke it stays open, so returning to service is not finishing the incident. Closure needs the eradication verified and recorded.
questions.hint: A working service says nothing about how it was broken.

options.text: 70 minutes, running from the confirmation at 23:05 through to the alert at 00:15.
35 minutes, counting only the part of the transfer that was stopped by hand.
options.misconception: counts only the portion the observer handled personally

options.text: 95 minutes, measured from the first outbound transfer at 22:40 to the alert.
options.misconception: starts the count at the first sign of transfer instead

options.text: 150 minutes, measured from the start of the observing session to the alert.
options.misconception: measures from the session start rather than the success

questions.explanation: From 23:05 to 00:15 is 70 minutes. The 22:40 entry is the first sign of the transfer, not the confirmed success, so it is not where the gap starts.
questions.hint: Start at the confirmed success, not the first sign of it.

questions.stem: The observatory's own dome log and the signal desk log both record the same evening. What does placing them on one timeline show that neither source shows on its own?

options.text: That the compromise began earlier than the dome log suggests, because the second source fills the gap.
That the two logs disagree about the date, so the whole evening should be discarded.
options.misconception: reads a timestamp mismatch as a reason to discard evidence

options.text: That the dome log is unreliable, because it records fewer events than the other source.
options.misconception: treats a smaller record count as proof the log is unreliable

options.text: That the signal desk saw everything, since its entries cover the entire period without breaks.
options.misconception: assumes the fuller source saw everything that happened

questions.explanation: Merging sources is done because each has blind spots. One source covers the period the other was silent, so a gap that looked like inactivity can turn out to be the start of the intrusion.

options.misconception: treats a routine mechanical delay as a sign of tampering

options.text: The weather station reports a late frost, which the keeper says can delay every mechanical part.
options.misconception: reads an unrelated frost delay as intrusion evidence

options.text: An observer mentions the coffee machine in the office was repaired on the same evening as the trace.
options.misconception: links an office repair to a trace with no shared link

options.text: A signed record shows a user account created during the intrusion, then used from a different country.

questions.explanation: Strength comes from specificity and linkage. A new account used from a distant place during the intrusion is tied to the event in time and method; a long settle or a frost is ordinary.

options.misconception: treats every change as equally meaningful

options.misconception: bases action on who was present rather than on evidence

Hunt for where the note was read, then reset the credential, then close the sessions it opened.

questions.hint: Cut off the working credential before hunting for the leak.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why the order of eradication work matters.
questions.stem: A volunteer found a compromised laptop in the education centre and wants to start tidying it at once. Explain why the order of the eradication work matters.

answer.exemplar: Order matters because each step assumes the previous one has held. Removal only makes sense once you know what you are removing, the check for persistence only means something once the process is gone, and rebuilding is worth doing only when the disk is known clean. Doing them out of order leaves you rebuilding a machine that is still compromised.

questions.explanation: Each step relies on the one before it, so doing them out of order means rebuilding a machine that is still compromised. A later step only means something once the earlier one held.

questions.topic: The order of the eradication work
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total time for a written eradication sequence.
questions.stem: A written eradication order for the clinic's shared workstation has four stages. Stage one took twenty-five minutes, stage two took fifteen, stage three took forty, and stage four took thirty. How many minutes did the four stages take in total?
questions.explanation: Twenty-five, fifteen, forty and thirty minutes add to one hundred and ten minutes for the four stages. The order matters too, since the rebuild is only safe after the hunt.
questions.hint: Add the four stage times together.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why removing one process is not the end of it
questions.learningObjective: Explain why removing one component does not close an intrusion.
questions.stem: A coffee shop's point-of-sale tablet was reset on 12 June. Explain why this single reset cannot be treated as the end of the problem.

answer.exemplar: A reset restores the tablet to a known state, but it says nothing about how the unwanted entry arrived, what else was changed while it was in use, or whether the route is still open for the next tablet on the same network. If the reset is also the only record kept, the reasoning behind it is lost, and the same access can return and leave a cleaner trail than before.

questions.explanation: A reset restores a device, not the route that reached it, and the entry and other changes go unrecorded unless written down. Without that record, the same access returns with less evidence.
questions.hint: A reset restores a device, not the route that reached it.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The order of bringing a service back
questions.learningObjective: Identify the step immediately before a service is reopened.

stimulus.body: The village clinic's booking service was restored on 3 May in this order. The server was rebuilt from its known-good image, the appointment records were copied back, the booking pages were checked with a test appointment, and only then was the phone line reopened for patients.

questions.stem: In the restoration plan above, which step came immediately before the phone line was reopened for patients?

options.text: Copying the appointment records back, because the records were the last thing restored.
options.misconception: puts the data copy directly before the reopening

options.text: Checking the booking pages with a test appointment, which confirmed the service worked.
Rebuilding the server from its known-good image, because that was the final technical step.
options.misconception: puts the rebuild directly before the reopening

options.text: Reopening the phone line straight after the rebuild, with no test of any kind.
options.misconception: skips the verification step in the plan

questions.explanation: The plan runs the test appointment and then reopens the line, so the test came directly before the patients came back. The rebuild and data copy happen earlier.
questions.hint: Read the final two steps of the restoration plan.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why bringing the service back is not the end
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a restored service does not end the incident.
questions.stem: The joinery workshop's job board is back online after the cleanup. Why is that not the end of the incident?

options.text: Because the job board should be rebuilt on new hardware before it is trusted again.
options.misconception: treats hardware replacement as the missing part of closure

options.text: Because two people must sign the closure before the workshop opens again.
options.misconception: replaces verification with a signing rule

options.text: Because the workshop must run the board cleanly for a month before closing.
options.misconception: sets a waiting period instead of verifying the eradication

options.text: Because the route in, the removal, and the evidence all still need settling in writing.

questions.explanation: A board that loads again shows only that it loads. The route in, the removal and the evidence still need settling, while new hardware and patience are house habit.
questions.hint: Ask whether route, removal and record are settled.
